lesson.title: Three Ways to Break the Rule: A Field Guide to Octet Exceptions
lesson.summary: Expanded octets, incomplete octets, and odd electron radicals are the three recognized categories of exceptions to the octet rule, and knowing all three lets you evaluate any Lewis structure with confidence instead of forcing every atom to fit eight electrons.
lesson.body:
Between expanded octets and incomplete octets, you have now met two of the three genuine categories of exceptions to the octet rule. Expanded octets happen when a period 3 or higher central atom, like sulfur in SF6 or phosphorus in PCl5, is surrounded by more than 8 electrons thanks to its accessible d subshell and larger size. Incomplete octets happen when an electron poor atom, like boron in BF3 or beryllium in BeCl2, cannot reach 8 electrons even with a sensible bonding pattern. Both are stable, real, correctly drawn Lewis structures, not mistakes.

The third category is different in kind: odd electron species, sometimes called free radicals. These arise whenever a molecule's total number of valence electrons is odd, which makes it mathematically impossible to pair every electron into bonding pairs and lone pairs, since both of those are counted in twos. One electron is always left unpaired. Nitrogen monoxide, NO, is a simple example: nitrogen contributes 5 valence electrons and oxygen contributes 6, for 11 total, an odd number. No matter how you arrange bonds and lone pairs, one electron in the structure has no partner.

Nitrogen dioxide, NO2, is a more commonly encountered odd electron molecule. Total valence electrons: nitrogen contributes 5 and two oxygens contribute 6 each, 12, for 17, again odd. NO2 is the reddish brown gas responsible for the visible haze in polluted air and one of the products of internal combustion engines. Its unpaired electron sits primarily on the nitrogen atom, and that unpaired electron is exactly why NO2 is so reactive: it readily pairs up with the unpaired electron of a second NO2 molecule to form dinitrogen tetroxide, N2O4, an ordinary, fully paired molecule.

Odd electron species cannot satisfy every atom's octet simultaneously, and that is expected, not a failure of the Lewis structure method. When you total a molecule's valence electrons and get an odd number, you already know before drawing anything that the structure will have one unpaired electron somewhere, usually placed on the less electronegative atom or the atom that gives the most reasonable formal charges. Radicals like NO and NO2 tend to be far more reactive than their fully paired counterparts precisely because that lone unpaired electron is eager to find a partner.

With all three categories in hand, expanded octets, incomplete octets, and odd electron radicals, you have a complete toolkit for recognizing when a molecule will not fit the simple eight electrons for every atom pattern. In practice, exceptions are identified the same way every other Lewis structure is built: count total valence electrons carefully, note the period of each atom for expanded octet potential, note how few valence electrons an atom like boron or beryllium brings for incomplete octet potential, and check whether the total electron count is odd for radical potential, before ever assuming something has gone wrong.
